**What this letter says**

"Our system has flagged IRREGULAR ACTIVITY on your government benefits file. Your SNAP, Medicaid, and Social Security accounts will be PERMANENTLY SUSPENDED within 48 hours unless a Compliance Reinstatement Fee of $500.00 is received."

In plain words: it claims something is wrong with your file, and that your benefits will be stopped for good unless you pay $500.00.

**What it asks you to do**

The letter says:
"(1) Purchase gift cards in the amount of $500.00 from any retail store. (2) Call our Enforcement Hotline at 555-0199 and read the card numbers to the compliance officer. (3) Do not discuss this matter with your caseworker, family, or bank, as your file is under a confidential federal investigation."

So it asks you to buy $500.00 in gift cards, call 555-0199, read the card numbers out loud, and keep this quiet from your caseworker, your family, and your bank.

**By when**

The letter says "within 48 hours." That is the only time limit printed. It does not print a date.

**What is missing from this letter**

Real notices about SNAP, Medicaid, or Social Security print things this letter does not print:

- No state or federal office address.
- No case number of your own — only "REF: FBE-2026-URGENT-9917."
- No reason with any detail — just "IRREGULAR ACTIVITY."
- No hearing rights. Real notices that stop or cut benefits tell you how to ask for a hearing and print a date.

**Where you can check**

Any real notice about your SNAP, Medicaid, or Social Security comes from your state benefits office or the Social Security office, and their phone numbers are printed on the letters they send you — not on this one. Gift cards are the part that gives it away. Once someone has the numbers off the back of a card, the money is gone, and there is no way to pull it back. That is exactly why scams ask for them.

**If you want to check on your own benefits**

Look at a real letter you have kept from your state benefits office or from Social Security, and use the phone number printed on that letter. Then you are calling a number you know is real, not one from this email. They can tell you whether anything is going on with your file.

That is a fair question. A badge number and a reference number look official — that is why they are there. But here is the thing about both: anyone can type them. Nothing about "Badge #4471" or "REF: FBE-2026-URGENT-9917" can be checked. There is no address, no office, no website, and no way to look either one up. If you want to be certain about your own file, the phone number on a real letter you already have will reach a real office. A free legal aid office can also look at this email beside one of your real letters and show you the difference, and their help costs nothing.

What is 'MAGI methodology'? That word is not in my dictionary.

Good question. It is not a normal English word — it is a short name used by the agency.

Here is the line again, as printed in your letter:

> "Your eligibility was determined using MAGI methodology under 42 CFR 435.603 based on the income information we verified electronically."

**"methodology"** — that is, the way of doing something; the set of steps used. So "MAGI methodology" means "the MAGI way of counting."

**MAGI** is made of the first letters of four words: Modified Adjusted Gross Income. In plain words:

- *Income* — the money you get.
- *Gross* — the whole amount, before anything is taken out.
- *Adjusted* and *Modified* — changed a little, by the program's rules, when they add it up.

So MAGI is a name for one certain way of adding up the money in your household for the year. Different programs count money in different ways. This is the way this program used for you.

The number **42 CFR 435.603** is where those counting rules are written down in law. Your letter points to it so you can see which rules were used.

Two things from your letter that go with this:

> "based on the income information we verified electronically"

They looked at money records they already had, through their computers, instead of asking you for papers.

> "You may request a copy of the information we used by calling 555-0177."

If you want to see the money numbers they used, the letter says you may call **555-0177** and ask for a copy.

If you want someone to go over how they counted your money, a free legal aid office can look at it with you.

That is what the letter says. Here is the line, as printed:

> "You do not need to send us anything at this time."

The letter is titled "NOTICE OF OVERPAYMENT" and is dated October 9, 2026. It says:

The letter lists things you can do. Here they are as printed:

> "You may ask us to waive collection if the overpayment was not your fault and you cannot afford to pay it back. There is no time limit to ask for a waiver."

A waiver, which means asking them to drop the debt so you do not pay it back, has no deadline in this letter.

> "You may appeal (ask for reconsideration) if you think the overpayment amount is wrong. You have 60 days from the date you receive this notice to appeal."

This is asking them to look at the amount again, if you believe $1,284.00 is not right.

> "If you appeal within 30 days — by November 9, 2026 — we will not change your monthly payment until we decide your case."

> "If you do nothing, we will withhold $73.00 from your monthly payment starting January 2027."

That last line means: if you do not act, they will take $73.00 out of each of your monthly payments, beginning in January 2027.

- To appeal: 60 days from the date you receive this notice.

**The appeal is about the number.**

The letter says:

> "You may appeal (ask for reconsideration) if you think the overpayment amount is wrong. You have 60 days from the date you receive this notice to appeal."

Here you are saying: *the amount is not right.* Maybe you think you were not overpaid at all, or that the amount is not $1,284.00. You are asking them to check their math and their facts again.

**The waiver is about paying it back.**

The letter says:

> "You may ask us to waive collection if the overpayment was not your fault and you cannot afford to pay it back. There is no time limit to ask for a waiver."

Here you are not arguing about the number. You are saying: *the overpayment happened, but it was not my fault, and I cannot afford to pay it back.* You are asking them to drop the debt.

**One short way to hold them apart**

- Waiver: "The amount may be right, but I should not have to pay it back."
